before: A diagram often needs a small item placed at a specific point. position: relative on a diagram creates a positioning reference for its absolutely positioned children in this example. position: absolute takes a child out of ordinary flow so top and left can place it relative to that reference. Give the diagram a width and height so you know what those percentages refer to. Moving a positioned item does not automatically push other content away; plan the diagram's space and labels carefully.

This fragment belongs inside body. It supplies the elements for the diagram CSS that follows. ```html
``` The outer div groups the diagram. class attributes let .diagram, .marker, and .pointer select their elements. A span is a general inline container; CSS can change how it is positioned and sized. These empty elements draw shapes when styled, but they do not explain the diagram's meaning. A real informative diagram also needs readable labels or a text description that explains what the shapes represent.

top: 50% places a child's top edge halfway down the reference area's height. left: 50% places its left edge halfway across the reference area's width. The reference here is the diagram's inner padding box, which excludes its border. In the standalone example, box-sizing: content-box explicitly gives that area a width of 320px and height of 180px, without padding, so the starting coordinates are 160px from its left and 90px from its top. They place an edge, not the child's center. To center a marker on that point, an additional translate(-50%, -50%) could shift it by half of its own dimensions. The exercise does not add that centering transform to its marker, so describe its location accurately.

A transform changes how an element is drawn. rotate(45deg) turns it by an angle. deg means degrees: a full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn is 180 degrees, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. translateX(6px) shifts along an x direction; scaling is a separate transform operation, outside this exercise. These are different operations. A transform does not make the surrounding layout recalculate as though the item had a new ordinary-flow size. A rotated pointer can therefore reach outside its original rectangle, so inspect its actual position and edges.

transform-origin chooses the pivot for rotation and scaling. 0 50% means the left edge and halfway down the element's own height. That gives a pointer a pivot near its starting end instead of its center. Transform order matters: rotate(45deg) translateX(6px) composes a translation followed by rotation, so the translation is rotated too and the pointer shifts along its turned direction. Reversing those function names changes the result. The percentages in transform-origin refer to the transformed element's box, while top and left percentages here use the containing reference area.

For the exercise, make .diagram relative with declared width: 300px and height: 200px, place .marker and .pointer absolutely with top and left at 50%, and give .pointer exactly rotate(30deg) translateX(8px) with origin 0 50%. The exercise runner uses border-box sizing: its 1px borders are included in those declared dimensions, leaving an inner reference area of 298px by 198px. Its midpoint is therefore 149px from the inner left edge and 99px from the inner top edge. The checks verify the declared canvas size, actual inner midpoint placement, intended transform, and left-edge midpoint pivot. At one size, fixed-pixel positions can look identical to percentages, so resize separately to check adaptation. Inspect the edges and explain the shapes' meaning; informative diagrams also need readable labels or a text description. This project builds a rotating diagram layout.
after: `position: relative` makes this diagram the reference box for its positioned children. Give it a width and height so there is a clear area to work in.
The supplied HTML has a diagram, a marker, and a pointer. The shapes show position. A useful diagram also needs words that explain what its shapes mean.

`top: 50%` and `left: 50%` place an item's top-left edge at the middle of the reference area. They do not put the item's own center there. The reference area here includes padding but excludes the border.
A transform changes how an element is drawn. `rotate(45deg)` turns it 45 degrees. A full turn is 360 degrees, so 90 degrees is a quarter turn. Nearby items do not move aside for the turned shape.
`transform-origin: 0 50%` puts the turning point at the middle of the pointer's left edge. With this transform order, the sideways shift is turned too. Reversing the functions changes the result.
For the project, make the diagram 300 by 200 pixels. Place both shapes at 50% from the top and left. Use `rotate(30deg) translateX(8px)` on the pointer, with its turning point at `0 50%`.

Set transform-origin to 0 50%. This makes the pointer turn around the middle of its left edge.

Position the marker and pointer absolutely at top 50% and left 50%.
Use `rotate(30deg) translateX(8px)` on the pointer in that order.
Put its turning point at `0 50%`, then run the checks.

before.question: What does `rotate(90deg)` do?
choices: Turns an element a quarter turn
before.explanation: A degree is an angle unit; 90 degrees is one quarter of a full 360-degree turn.

after.question: What does rotate(90deg) do?
choices: Turns an element a quarter turn
after.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees. Ninety degrees is one quarter of that.
